items.title: Antidepressant effects have been distorted by publication bias
items.claim: Turner et al.'s 2008 NEJM analysis compared published antidepressant trials with those registered with the FDA. What did they find?

options.text: Of 74 registered trials, 38 positive trials were nearly all published (37/38) while 36 negative or questionable trials were largely unpublished or recast as positive — inflating apparent efficacy by ~32%

items.reveal_title: What's published is not what's done
items.reveal:
Turner, Matthews, Linardatos, Tell & Rosenthal (NEJM 2008) used FDA records covering 12 antidepressants. Cipriani et al. (Lancet 2018) meta-analysed all available antidepressant trials and found small but real effect sizes, with substantial variation between drugs.

Resulting reforms: ClinicalTrials.gov pre-registration (2007 US law); EU mandatory reporting; the AllTrials campaign. Bias has reduced but not disappeared.
items.why: Evidence-based medicine depends on the available evidence being representative. Publication bias systematically distorts apparent treatment effects.

items.title: Re-evaluating Stanford Prison
items.claim: Philip Zimbardo's 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment is often cited as proof that situations dictate behaviour. What did later archival work by Le Texier and others reveal?

options.text: Guards received explicit coaching, undermining the 'natural' interpretation
No participant played the guard role

items.reveal_title: Guards were coached, not spontaneously behaving
items.reveal:
Le Texier's 2018 archival analysis and a 2019 American Psychologist article showed guards received briefings encouraging tough behaviour.

The BBC Prison Study (Reicher & Haslam, 2006) produced very different dynamics under similar setup.
items.why: Replication and archival work reshape how landmark findings are interpreted.
